strengths: The paper tackles a relevant problem in dense RGB-D SLAM: improving neural implicit and 3DGS-based SLAM with higher-level visual features rather than relying only on color/depth losses.

The central idea of using DINO-derived continuous features as supervision or Gaussian attributes is plausible and potentially useful, especially because it avoids semantic labels and fixed taxonomies.

The submission evaluates both NeRF-style and 3DGS-style variants across standard SLAM benchmarks: Replica, ScanNet, and TUM RGB-D. The experiments cover tracking, reconstruction, rendering, memory, runtime, and several ablations.

The generality ablation is a useful aspect: the authors show gains when adding the proposed feature strategy to multiple representations, including hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, and 3D Gaussian Splatting.
The paper is generally readable and well organized, with clear high-level motivation and helpful architectural figures.
weaknesses: I view the work as primarily Applied/Systems rather than a pure algorithmic contribution: the main contribution is an integration strategy for DINO features into existing SLAM pipelines. Under that lens the evidence is relevant, but the paper needs stronger system detail and fairness analysis to be convincing.

The technical description of the Scene Structure Encoder is underspecified. It is unclear whether the MLPs and attention blocks are pretrained, optimized online per scene, frozen, or jointly trained with the SLAM system. This also conflicts somewhat with the claim of requiring no offline training, since DINO is pretrained and the status of SSE training is not made precise.

Several equations and tensor relationships are unclear. For example, the loss comparing tri-plane encodings directly to EDINO features does not specify dimensional alignment, sampling locations, feature resolutions, or how per-pixel/image features supervise a 3D representation. The 3DGS formulation says EDINO features are assigned into Gaussian parameters, but the initialization, update rule, dimensionality, and memory/runtime consequences are not sufficiently specified.

The empirical claims are somewhat overstated. The method is not uniformly best: on Replica some baselines are better on accuracy or depth L1; on ScanNet PLGSLAM reports a better average ATE than the NeRF variant; on TUM MonoGS is better on some individual sequences. The text sometimes states consistent or state-of-the-art superiority beyond what the tables support.

Fairness of comparison is not fully established. The paper integrates global bundle adjustment and DINO supervision into some variants, but it is not always clear which improvements come from DINO/EDINO versus engineering choices such as BA, keyframe selection, or baseline-specific implementation differences.

Runtime analysis is incomplete. Extracting DINO features can be expensive, yet the FPS and memory table does not clearly state whether DINO/SSE inference time, feature storage, and preprocessing are included. This is important for SLAM, where real-time viability is central.

The ablations show improvements but many gains are modest, especially in the generality table. The paper would benefit from stronger analysis of when DINO features help or fail, sensitivity to loss weights and feature resolution, and robustness under dynamic objects, lighting changes, or loop closure scenarios.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details: feature dimensions, DINO layer choice, SSE architecture sizes, optimization schedule, sampling strategy for feature losses, and exact integration details for each adapted baseline are not sufficiently documented.

The paper does not discuss limitations or failure cases in meaningful depth. The conclusion briefly mentions future loop closure and sub-mapping, but there is little analysis of scalability, drift in long trajectories, dynamic scenes, computational cost, or dependence on pretrained feature quality.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving dense RGB-D SLAM with stronger scene-level priors, and it studies both implicit NeRF-style and explicit 3DGS-style representations under one framework.
The experimental section covers standard SLAM benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) and reports several relevant metrics for tracking, reconstruction, rendering, runtime, and memory.
The idea of using self-supervised DINO features as a category-free signal is practically appealing, especially compared with semantic-SLAM methods that require labels or predefined classes.
The ablations attempt to separate raw DINO features, the proposed EDINO/SSE features, and bundle adjustment, which is the right direction for validating the claim.
weaknesses: The technical description is not sufficiently convincing. The Scene Structure Encoder is introduced as central, but its training/optimization procedure is unclear: whether the MLPs and attention modules are pretrained, optimized online, frozen, or jointly learned is not specified well enough to reproduce or assess the method. This also conflicts with the claim of no offline training.

Several equations and representations are underspecified or dimensionally ambiguous. For example, the L1 supervision between tri-plane encodings and EDINO features is not clearly defined spatially or dimensionally, and the 3DGS formulation says EDINO is incorporated into Gaussian parameters but the Gaussian equation itself is unchanged and does not explain how those features affect geometry, color, opacity, or tracking.

The experimental gains are often small or mixed relative to strong baselines. On Replica, the NeRF variant is not best in accuracy, depth L1, or tracking RMSE compared with Point-SLAM; on ScanNet, PLGSLAM remains better than the proposed NeRF variant; and many reported 3DGS rendering improvements are marginal.

The 3DGS comparison is difficult to interpret because the method also adopts global BA/keyframe strategies from other work. Since tracking uses color/depth residuals only, it is unclear whether improvements come from DINO/EDINO features or from engineering choices such as BA, thresholds, and baseline reimplementation details.

The ablations do not fully support the broad claims. In Table 5, removing EDINO from the 3DGS variant changes PSNR/SSIM/depth only minimally, while the large tracking changes are not clearly causally tied to DINO features. Table 4 mostly shows modest improvements and uses heterogeneous metrics across baselines, making the claimed generality weaker than stated.

The paper overclaims superiority. Statements such as consistently outperforming all existing methods are not supported by the tables, where the proposed method is not consistently best across datasets, metrics, or representation families.

Important reproducibility details are missing: exact DINO feature resolution/layer, feature normalization, SSE architecture sizes, optimization schedule, computational cost of DINO extraction, code availability, per-scene variance, and whether baseline numbers are reproduced or taken from papers.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations discussion. Practical issues such as runtime overhead from DINO extraction, memory scaling for storing feature channels, behavior in dynamic/outdoor scenes, loop closure absence, and sensitivity to depth noise are not analyzed despite being central for SLAM deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving RGB-D neural SLAM by injecting stronger scene-level priors from self-supervised DINO features. The contribution is relevant to computer vision and robotics, and the idea is well motivated by limitations of purely photometric/geometric supervision.

A notable strength is the generality of the proposed design. The method is instantiated for both NeRF-style implicit representations and 3D Gaussian Splatting, and Table 4 further shows gains when adding the DINO/SSE idea to several different encodings, including hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, and 3DGS.

The experimental evidence is broad for a SLAM paper: Replica, ScanNet, and TUM are all evaluated, with tracking, reconstruction, rendering, model size, and runtime metrics. The results are consistently favorable, especially for Replica reconstruction/completion and TUM/ScanNet trajectory accuracy.

The ablations are useful and support the main claim that raw DINO features alone are helpful but that the proposed enhanced DINO features from the Scene Structure Encoder provide additional benefit. This strengthens the scientific case beyond simply attaching an off-the-shelf feature loss.

The paper is generally clear and easy to follow. The figures communicate the two pipelines well, and the method section explains how DINO/EDINO supervision is incorporated into the NeRF and 3DGS variants.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but not fully transformative. The main idea is to integrate self-supervised DINO features into existing neural SLAM pipelines, and much of the system design builds directly on established NeRF-SLAM and 3DGS-SLAM machinery. The paper would benefit from a sharper discussion of what is fundamentally new beyond feature distillation and feature-augmented supervision.

Some methodological details are underspecified for reproducibility. For example, the training or optimization status of the Scene Structure Encoder is not completely clear, nor are all architecture dimensions, update schedules, feature resolutions, and computational costs of DINO/SSE extraction described in enough detail to enable confident reimplementation.

The fairness of comparisons is somewhat hard to judge. The method is integrated into strong baselines, but the exact relation between the reported systems and their original implementations is not always clear, and some baselines may use different post-processing, semantic inputs, bundle adjustment strategies, or scene-specific tuning.

The runtime results temper the practical impact. The NeRF variant is slower than several alternatives, and the 3DGS variant is around 0.61 FPS in the reported setting, which is far from real-time despite the SLAM framing. More discussion of deployment constraints, latency from DINO feature extraction, and memory/runtime tradeoffs would be valuable.

The 3DGS ablation table reports much lower PSNR/SSIM than the main Replica rendering table, apparently because it is on ScanNet, but this shift makes the ablation less directly interpretable. More consistent per-dataset ablations would make the evidence cleaner.

The evaluation is mostly limited to standard indoor RGB-D benchmarks. Since the paper emphasizes robustness and higher-level scene understanding, additional stress tests on dynamic scenes, lighting changes, texture-poor areas, loop closure, or larger-scale environments would better substantiate the broader claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: improving dense RGB-D SLAM systems based on NeRF and Gaussian Splatting using foundation-model features. The core idea of making DINO features geometry-aware through depth-conditioned attention is well motivated for SLAM, where vanilla image features lack explicit 3D structure.

A notable strength is generality. The proposed SGE/geoDINO design is integrated into several representation families, including hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D Gaussian surfels, with consistent gains reported over the corresponding baselines.

The experimental coverage is broad for an Algorithms/General paper: Replica, ScanNet, and TUM RGB-D are all used, with evaluation of tracking, reconstruction, rendering, runtime, memory, ablations, and a small depth-noise robustness study.

The ablations are useful and directly support the central claim: vanilla DINO helps modestly, simple DINO-depth concatenation helps slightly more, and the proposed geoDINO features provide larger gains in both NeRF and GS settings.

Results are generally strong. The GS variant in particular improves over GauS-SLAM on Replica rendering/tracking and ScanNet/TUM tracking, while adding little overhead in the reported GS setting. The qualitative results also align with the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The work is best viewed as a well-engineered feature-conditioning and auxiliary-supervision paradigm for existing SLAM backbones, rather than a fundamentally new SLAM formulation. Prior work already explores DINO/semantic features in neural SLAM; the main distinction is the depth-aware SGE and its systematic integration.

Important implementation details are underspecified. The paper does not sufficiently clarify feature dimensionalities, attention resolution, how geoDINO is associated with and updated for each Gaussian over time, how losses are scheduled during tracking versus mapping, or whether all integrations use identical hyperparameter tuning budgets. This could limit reproducibility.

Some claims are overstated. The method is not uniformly state of the art: PLGSLAM has a better ScanNet average than the NeRF variant, SNI-SLAM has better Replica tracking RMSE than the NeRF variant, and some TUM sequences are won by other methods. The contribution remains strong, but the text sometimes frames the gains too broadly.

Fairness of comparison is not fully established. Several baselines appear to be taken from prior papers or author-provided outputs, and not all competing methods are evaluated under identical hardware, code, post-processing, and keyframe settings. This matters because the reported gains over strong baselines can be relatively small for tracking metrics.

The computational analysis is mixed. The GS overhead is reported as negligible, but the NeRF variant roughly halves FPS relative to ESLAM and increases memory substantially. The cost of extracting DINOv2 features and running SGE in realistic online settings deserves more explicit discussion.

The robustness analysis is limited to one Replica scene with synthetic Gaussian depth noise. Since the method relies directly on RGB-D depth to construct geoDINO features, more evidence under real sensor noise, missing depth, dynamic objects, and outdoor or large-scale scenes would strengthen the claims.

The paper provides limited discussion of failure modes and limitations. For example, cases where DINO semantics may be misleading, where depth is sparse/noisy, or where online SGE optimization destabilizes tracking are not analyzed in depth.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for RGB-D neural SLAM: improving mapping, rendering, and tracking by injecting stronger semantic/structural priors into NeRF- and Gaussian-splatting-based systems.

The proposed framework is evaluated on several standard benchmarks, including Replica, ScanNet, and TUM RGB-D, and the paper reports improvements over the chosen ESLAM and GauS-SLAM backbones on many metrics.
The authors attempt to show generality by integrating the idea into multiple scene encodings, including hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D Gaussian surfels.

The ablation comparing no DINO, vanilla DINO, concatenated DINO-depth, and geoDINO is useful and supports the claim that simply adding frozen DINO features is less effective than the proposed geometry-aware variant.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core idea is to distill or embed DINO/DINOv2 features into neural SLAM representations and modulate them with depth via attention, which feels like an incremental combination of existing foundation-model feature distillation, semantic SLAM, and RGB-D neural SLAM rather than a clearly new algorithmic advance.

The method is under-specified in important ways. The SGE is said to be optimized online, but the paper does not clearly explain what prevents the geoDINO targets from drifting, how gradients flow through the frozen DINO branch versus the learned SGE components, the dimensionalities/resolutions of the feature maps, or how features are aligned with NeRF samples and Gaussian primitives in practice.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, the NeRF variant is not best on several Replica metrics, is worse than SNI-SLAM on Replica RMSE, and is behind PLGSLAM on ScanNet average ATE. The paper repeatedly frames the results as broadly state-of-the-art despite these mixed outcomes.

The reported gains are often modest, especially for tracking, and no variance, multiple-run statistics, or significance analysis is provided. This is concerning because SLAM results can be sensitive to initialization, keyframe selection, implementation details, and sequence-level randomness.

The experimental comparison is not fully convincing. Table 1 mixes different metrics across papers and encodings, some baselines use special supervision such as ground-truth semantic masks, and it is unclear whether all baselines were reproduced under identical settings or copied from prior work. This weakens the fairness of the generality claim.

The computational analysis is somewhat confusing. The NeRF variant nearly halves FPS relative to ESLAM and increases memory substantially, yet the paper emphasizes negligible overhead. It is also unclear whether the cost of DINO feature extraction, storage, and online SGE optimization is consistently included across all comparisons.

The GS formulation is not very well motivated technically. Assigning geoDINO features to Gaussian parameters and supervising rendered features with vanilla DINO features is described at a high level, but the paper does not give enough detail to understand why this should improve geometry and tracking beyond acting as an auxiliary regularizer.

The robustness experiment is narrow: only one Replica scene and one synthetic Gaussian depth-noise setting are tested. Since the method depends on depth to build geoDINO features, stronger evaluation under real sensor noise, missing depth, dynamic objects, and larger-scale trajectories would be needed.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details such as training schedules, optimizer settings, feature resolutions, feature normalization, exact loss balancing across backbones, keyframe/window settings for all integrated systems, and whether code or precomputed features will be released.

The paper has presentation issues in several tables and formulas, including cramped entries, inconsistent naming of '+DINO' versus geoDINO, and occasional over-general wording. These do not invalidate the work, but they make the technical case harder to audit.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and active problem in dense RGB-D SLAM: improving neural implicit and explicit scene representations beyond low-level photometric and depth losses. The central idea of injecting geometry-aware DINO features into both NeRF- and Gaussian-splatting-based SLAM systems is well motivated and relevant to ECCV.

The proposed framework is unusually broad in scope. The authors do not only modify one backbone, but show integration with hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D Gaussian surfels. This supports the claim that the contribution is a general SLAM design paradigm rather than a narrow model-specific trick.

The experimental evidence is strong overall. Results on Replica, ScanNet, and TUM RGB-D show consistent gains in reconstruction, rendering, and tracking metrics, and the ablations separate vanilla DINO, simple DINO-depth concatenation, and the proposed geoDINO features. The gains over already strong GS baselines such as GauS-SLAM are particularly compelling.

The paper includes useful efficiency analysis. Reporting FPS, memory footprint, and an SGE runtime breakdown makes the practical cost of the method clearer; the GS variant appears to add little overhead relative to the baseline while improving accuracy.
The manuscript is generally clear and well structured, with helpful pipeline figures and a coherent connection between motivation, method, ablations, and benchmark comparisons.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental. The method combines DINO/DINOv2 features, RGB-D geometry, attention-style fusion, and feature-supervised neural SLAM, all of which are plausible extensions of recent semantic/foundation-model-assisted SLAM work. The main value is breadth and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new SLAM formulation.

Some technical details are underspecified. The dimensional alignment and spatial correspondence between geoDINO features and tri-plane features in the NeRF loss are not fully clear, and the GS pipeline’s use of geoDINO as Gaussian parameters while supervising rendered features with vanilla DINO would benefit from a more precise optimization description.

The evaluation is broad but still limited to standard indoor RGB-D benchmarks. The method is not tested on dynamic scenes, outdoor scenes, severe lighting changes, long-term relocalization, or loop-closure-heavy trajectories, which limits confidence in the broader autonomous-systems claims.

Real-time practicality remains mixed. The GS variant has negligible overhead over GauS-SLAM, but the absolute FPS values are still low for many robotics settings, and the NeRF variant roughly halves ESLAM’s FPS. The paper should temper claims about deployment or discuss where this computational profile is acceptable.

Comparisons rely on heterogeneous baselines and reported settings, including author-provided meshes and methods with different capabilities such as semantic supervision, bundle adjustment, and scene scaling. More controlled re-runs or a clearer fairness discussion would strengthen the case.

The robustness analysis is useful but narrow: only Gaussian depth noise on one Replica scene is reported. Since the method explicitly depends on depth to construct geometry-aware DINO features, more systematic depth-noise, missing-depth, sensor-domain, and calibration-error studies would be valuable.
